AK-2025-HB10.s: The bill would change how the University of Alaska Board of Regents is set up and how some members are chosen. It would require at least one regent to be a current tenured faculty member chosen from a list of faculty nominees, and it would change the board’s quorum rules, which set how many members must be present to act. Some parts would take effect on February 1, 2033.

AK-2025-HB110.s: This bill would make changes to health care licensing rules in Alaska, including for doctors, physician assistants, psychologists, social workers, respiratory care, and EMS workers. It would also join or update several interstate compacts, which are agreements with other states that help professionals get licensed across state lines. The bill would add rules for criminal history checks, telehealth for respiratory care, school asthma and anaphylaxis care plans, and group health insurance rules for respiratory care practitioners, and it would create a Rural Health Transformation Program Advisory Council.

AK-2025-HB117.s: The law lets Alaska require electronic monitoring on certain state commercial finfish trawl boats, but only if the boats already have the needed gear for a federal fishery and no extra cost is shifted to fishers. It also creates a separate management area on the east side of Cook Inlet for some commercial set net permits, with rules to move or renew permits in that area starting in 2027. Some parts took effect right away, and the rest take effect as stated in the law.

AK-2025-HB126.s: The law lets some Alaska Native village corporations that were involuntarily dissolved be reinstated at any time, instead of only within two years. It also changes what proxy voting papers and other shareholder materials must be filed with the state for certain Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act corporations. The law took effect on June 25, 2026.

AK-2025-HB13.s: The bill would let Alaska cities and towns give optional property tax breaks for certain homes and rental properties, including places used by volunteer fire, emergency medical, paramedic, and hazardous materials responders. It also covers some long-term rental units, mobile home parks, homes rented to low-income families, a person’s main home, and homes bought by first-time buyers. The bill also changes how towns refund overpaid or wrongly paid property taxes by setting a new interest rule.

AK-2025-HB133.s: The bill would set payment deadlines for state contract work, and it would add interest if an agency pays late or gives a late notice for withheld payment. It would also set payment deadlines for grants and reimbursement agreements to nonprofit groups, municipalities, and Alaska Native organizations, with some rules tied to federal funds. In addition, it would require state agencies to report late payments made during 2026 and would expand the state financial transactions website to show more public spending and payment details.

AK-2025-HB14.s: The law requires health insurers, including municipal plans, to cover telehealth services the same way they cover in-person care, at least at the same rate. It also changes workers' compensation rules for certain firefighters by expanding the list of covered diseases and extending the time a claim can be presumed covered. The law raises some disability and retiree medical benefits for public employees and removes some state programs for certain medical aid. It took effect under the chapter law provisions listed in the bill.

AK-2025-HB16.s: The bill would require some groups that support or oppose a candidate or ballot measure in Alaska elections to keep a physical address in the state or use an in-state agent. It would raise campaign donation limits for state and local offices, and the Alaska Public Offices Commission would adjust those limits every 10 years starting in 2031 based on inflation. It would also change reporting and complaint rules for election complaints, and it would set rules for spending and donations by foreign-influenced corporations and foreign nationals.

AK-2025-HB173.s: The bill would update Alaska rules for licensing occupational therapists, occupational therapy assistants, physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, audiologists, and speech-language pathologists. It would add a new executive administrator for the State Physical Therapy and Occupational Therapy Board and require national criminal history checks for some license and compact privilege applications. It would also create an occupational therapy licensure compact, which lets qualified therapists work across state lines under that agreement.

AK-2025-HB176.s: The bill would require the University of Alaska to email students before it adds a new required fee or raises one, and to explain the amount, why it is being charged, and how the money will be used. It would also require the university to give each student a billing statement that lists tuition and fees separately. The bill would take effect July 1, 2027.

AK-2025-HB184.s: This law lets the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority help finance new workforce housing projects with three or more homes. It also adds certain housing assets of the authority to a required exemption from city property taxes. The law took effect on September 16, 2026.

AK-2025-HB195.s: The law changes the name “physician assistant” to “physician associate” in Alaska rules and updates related medical board and licensing laws. It also changes rules for pharmacists, including collaborative practice agreements, and lets pharmacists take part in some drug and device prescribing and reciprocity rules. The law also requires prescribers to offer an opioid overdose drug in certain opioid cases and sets an effective date.

AK-2025-HB216.s: The bill approved the Alaska Railroad Corporation’s transfer of about 84.8 acres of rail land in Whittier to the City of Whittier. The land may be sold for fair market value, or swapped for land or cash of equal value, and the railroad and the city must handle any needed surveying and platting. It became law without the governor’s signature on June 30, 2026, and took effect on July 3, 2026.

AK-2025-HB221.s: Alaska Arts and Culture Day is established for the first Friday of every October. Schools, community groups, and other public and private groups and people may mark it with events and activities that build awareness and appreciation of arts and culture in the state. The measure became law on June 30, 2026, and took effect on July 4, 2026.

AK-2025-HB23.s: The bill would rename Alaska’s State Commission for Human Rights as the Alaska State Commission for Civil Rights. It would change rules on how the commission investigates complaints, removes commissioners, reports each year, and defines who counts as an employer, and it would also update how local civil rights commissions work. The act would take effect on January 1, 2027.

AK-2025-HB239.s: The bill would change Alaska laws on many crimes and court rules, including murder, assault, sexual assault, stalking, child abuse, theft, prostitution, and drug crimes. It would also update rules for victims who were abused as minors, child testimony in criminal cases, sexual assault exam kits, parole, school bus driver licensing, and the address confidentiality program. Some changes would raise the age cutoffs for certain crimes involving minors from under 16 to under 18.

AK-2025-HB243.s: The measure changes the powers and duties of Alaska’s Board of Barbers and Hairdressers and the state commerce department. It says the board can examine license applicants, help authorize licenses and permits, make rules, and ask for investigations or hold hearings in some cases. It also sets a 12-hour training rule for manicuring school licenses and became law on 7/3/26.

AK-2025-HB244.s: This act updates the training rules for certified nurse aides in Alaska. It would require training programs to teach safe and competent care, good communication, respect for a client’s rights and dignity, and care for people with memory loss, dementia, or other mental health or cognitive needs. The law takes effect January 1, 2027.

AK-2025-HB249.s: The law changes how a vehicle can be transferred to an insurance company after damage is paid. It says the papers for that transfer do not need to be notarized and can be signed online and printed. It applies to registered vehicles and to forms like a power of attorney, duplicate title, and odometer disclosure forms. The law takes effect on 10/18/26.

AK-2025-HB25.s: The bill would bar restaurants from serving prepared food in polystyrene foam food containers, and it would also stop the state from using or buying them. It would let customers bring clean containers for food if state rules set steps to avoid cross-contamination, and it would allow some exceptions for outside-the-state food, disaster areas, and local rules. It would take effect on January 1, 2027, and it was later vetoed by the governor.

AK-2025-HB262.s: The bill would increase the number of superior court judges in Alaska’s third judicial district from 28 to 29. It would take effect on July 1, 2026.

AK-2025-HB263.s: The bill would fund state government operating and loan program costs for fiscal year 2027, and it would also adjust some past appropriations and add some extra funding. It covers many state departments and programs, including administration, commerce, corrections, and other state services. The measure also includes some instructions to agencies, such as plans for payroll work and requests for information on possible out-of-state prison housing.

AK-2025-HB265.s: The bill would set aside money for Alaska’s mental health program for the fiscal year starting July 1, 2026, and ending June 30, 2027. It covers operating and capital costs for state agencies, the court system, and the University of Alaska, and includes $454,500 for expanded early intervention services. The latest version also says the law would take effect on July 1, 2026.

AK-2025-HB27.s: The bill would require the state education department to set up hands-only CPR lessons for public school students and decide which grade levels must get them. It would also let certain certified instructors, emergency medical workers, and teachers teach the lessons, if practical. The bill would also update state rules for emergency medical care, including adding heart attack and stroke to the meaning of a major emergency. Sections 1 and 2 would take effect July 1, 2027.

AK-2025-HB278.s: The bill would create the Alaska-Ireland Trade Commission in the Department of Commerce, Community, and Economic Development. The group would have five governor appointees, two House members, and two Senate members, and it would work on trade, investment, business, research, and school exchanges between Alaska and Ireland. It would also set meeting rules, reporting duties, and allow grants or gifts to help pay some costs; the act would take effect right away.

AK-2025-HB28.s: The bill would change several Alaska school rules, including school funding, school board membership, substitute teaching, and correspondence study materials. It would let some students keep certain materials after leaving a correspondence program, and it would allow a regional school board member to work as a substitute teacher in short-term emergency cases. It would also set up a pilot program to help teachers repay student loans and create a state payment for school district energy costs based on past fuel and electricity spending.

AK-2025-HB280.s: The measure would update Alaska’s rules for dividing business income for tax purposes and add the Multistate Tax Compact into state law. It would affect multistate businesses, including broadcasters, financial firms, and phone and telecom providers, by setting how their income is assigned to Alaska and other places. The bill was transmitted to the governor and later vetoed.

AK-2025-HB298.s: The law changes Alaska's legislative ethics rules for legislators and legislative employees. It updates limits on using state resources, adds protections for people who report possible violations, and changes gift disclosure rules. It also changes the make-up and staffing rules for the legislative ethics committee and takes effect on June 24, 2026.

AK-2025-HB3001.s: This bill would change tax rules for certain natural gas project property and related facilities, and it would set rules for a natural gas project’s ties to local school funding and city taxes. It would also change reporting rules for pipeline projects, create an affordable heating fuel fund, and create a municipal impact grant program and fund. The bill would also address Alaska Gasline Development Corporation funds, contract approval by the state utility commission, and a possible alternative tax on natural gas flow, and it includes an effective date.

AK-2025-HB3002.s: The bill would end Alaska’s income tax on pass-through businesses, which are businesses that pass profits through to the owners’ personal taxes. It would repeal the current law on January 1, 2028.

AK-2025-HB302.s: Passed law changes Alaska insurance rules for travel insurance, insurance licensing, rebates, and advertising. It adds rules for how travel insurers report and pay premium taxes, and it gives the insurance director more licensing and oversight powers. It also updates some exceptions to anti-rebate rules and includes changes tied to unemployment benefits.

AK-2025-HB314.s: The bill would add rules for registered interior designers and let some people do interior design work without using that title unless they are registered. It would also change the state board that oversees architects, engineers, land surveyors, landscape architects, and interior designers, including extending its end date to 2033 and updating its membership. The measure would also change how project costs are counted for airports and some other public projects, and it would set an effective date.

AK-2025-HB36.s: The bill updates rules for treatment foster homes and for children in state custody who need psychiatric care. It lets the state place some children in a hospital or residential psychiatric treatment center for short-term mental health care, with court review and notice to the child, family, and other parties. It also changes related duties for the Department of Family and Community Services and a court rule, and it became law with an effective date the same as passage.

AK-2025-HB363.s: This law changes who can buy or serve alcohol under club and nonprofit event permits in Alaska. It lets patriotic groups, such as the American Legion, Veterans of Foreign Wars, and American Veterans organizations, sell or serve some alcoholic drinks at their events, and it adds those groups to the law on club licenses. It took effect on June 19, 2026.

AK-2025-HB381.s: The bill would change how some natural gas project property is taxed and would create new taxes and funds tied to oil and gas work in Alaska. It would also change how local school funding is figured, including the required local contribution from city and borough school districts. The measure also deals with municipal property taxes, reporting for natural gas pipeline projects, and approval of certain contracts and natural gas prices.

AK-2025-HB388.s: This law raises the loan limit from Alaska’s bulk fuel loan account and bulk fuel bridge loan account to $1.5 million per borrower. For some cooperative groups that buy fuel for more than one community, the bulk fuel loan amount can be multiplied by the number of communities served. It also lets the state use money from the bulk fuel revolving loan fund to cover these loans in fiscal years 2026 and 2027 if the fund balance is not enough, and it took effect on July 3, 2026.

AK-2025-HB39.s: The bill became law and applies to public school students in Alaska who are deaf or hard of hearing, or may be. It requires school districts to give parents clear information about hearing tools, ways to communicate, and related services, and to follow the parent’s chosen communication method when providing services. It also directs the state to support one or more programs for deaf students, including possible residential services, and sets rules for school districts that run such programs.

AK-2025-HB48.s: The bill would change how Alaska’s civil legal services fund is financed. It would let lawmakers put into the fund up to 25 percent of court filing fees from the prior year, and the fund could be used to pay groups that provide civil legal help to low-income people. A low-income person is defined as someone with income at or below 125 percent of the federal poverty level for Alaska.

AK-2025-HB50.s: The bill would change the state rule for a "snow classic," a game of chance where people guess how much snow is on the ground at a set place and time to win a cash prize. It would remove the old limit that tied this game to Mount Alyeska and one named nonprofit group. The law took effect on 9/21/26.

AK-2025-HB52.s: The bill would give minors at psychiatric hospitals the right to weekly private phone or video time with a parent, guardian, or other approved adult, unless a court order, law, or medical judgment says no. It would require hospitals to report each use of seclusion or restraint on a minor to the Department of Health and the parent or guardian within 72 hours, and the department would publish a yearly report on these cases and related inspections. It would also require unannounced inspections of certain psychiatric hospitals at least twice a year and take effect on July 1, 2027.

AK-2025-HB79.s: The bill would rename the University of Alaska’s Institute of Social and Economic Research as the Vic Fischer Institute of Social and Economic Research. It would also name a state marine park unit Vic Fischer Shoup Bay State Marine Park. The text says the university should not spend money just to change signs or materials for the new institute name; the bill was later vetoed by the governor.

AK-2025-HB93.s: The bill would change the residency rules for hunting, trapping, and sport fishing privileges in Alaska. It would require people with a permanent ID card to still meet the state’s resident rules, and it would update the rules for who counts as a resident when applying for a license. The state fish and game commissioner would also have to set rules for checking if someone qualifies as a resident, and the law would take effect on January 1, 2028.

AK-2025-HB96.s: The bill would create a Home Care Employment Standards Advisory Board in the health department to review pay rates, worker wages, working conditions, and service levels for home care and related services. It would also require agencies to spend set shares of their personal care service funding on employee pay and benefits: at least 70% starting July 1, 2027, and 80% starting July 1, 2030, with lower first-step amounts and later deadlines for some hardship cases. The board would have to meet by October 1, 2027, and the pay rules would take effect only if federal approval is given or not needed by January 1, 2027.

AK-2025-HCR12.s: The resolution would suspend certain Alaska Legislature rules so Senate Bill 64 could have its title changed. It affects the handling of that bill, which deals with elections, voting, voter registration, election administration, campaign contributions, and related crimes.

AK-2025-HCR16.s: The resolution would suspend certain Alaska Legislature rules so Senate Bill 230 could move forward. That bill is about the boundaries of the Jonesville Public Use Area. It affects the handling of that land boundary bill in the legislature.

AK-2025-HCR23.s: The resolution would suspend some Alaska Legislature rules about bill title changes for Senate Bill 29. That bill is about an executive administrator for the Big Game Commercial Services Board. It passed and was transmitted to the governor.

AK-2025-HCR301.s: This resolution would suspend two Alaska Legislature rules so certain bills could carry over to a special session. It applies only to House Bill 381, which deals with taxes on some natural gas pipeline property and related local tax limits. It is retroactive to June 20, 2026, at 10:00 a.m., the start of the third special session.

AK-2025-HCR4.s: The Alaska Legislature would proclaim May 2026 as Myositis Awareness Month. It also encourages residents to learn about myositis, a rare muscle disease, and to support people and families affected by it.

AK-2025-HCR9.s: The resolution would honor the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence and the founding of the United States. It would encourage people, schools, civic groups, and businesses in Alaska to take part in events that reflect on U.S. history and core ideals. It would also encourage schools to strengthen civics education so students learn about civic participation, federalism, and self-government.

AK-2025-HJR18.s: This resolution says Alaska lawmakers support a natural gas pipeline project and want federal agencies to speed up approvals and review. It also asks for federal help with coordination and funding for the project. The measure affects the state pipeline project and the federal offices named in it.

AK-2025-HJR20.s: The Alaska Legislature adopted a resolution that asks Congress to set hiring goals for apprentices and veteran apprentices on U.S. Defense Department construction projects in the United States. It would call for at least 20 percent of the workforce on those projects to be in apprenticeship or postsecondary programs. It would also call for at least 10 percent of those apprentices or students in each job class to be veterans.

AK-2025-HJR28.s: This resolution asks Congress to pass the Kids Online Safety Act. The act would require some online platforms to add safety tools for users under 17, give parents more controls, and add more public reporting and checks. It also would limit certain data use and set up an advisory council on risks to minors online.

AK-2025-HJR32.s: The Alaska Legislature would express support for the rural health transformation program and call attention to health care problems in rural parts of the state. It notes that Alaska received $272,174,856 for the first year of the program and says the money should help with care access, health workers, telehealth, and health system updates. The measure urges the Governor and Alaska’s members of Congress to work for the state’s interests and protect the full funding award.

AK-2025-HJR38.s: This resolution would urge the U.S. Congress to recognize public safety telecommunicators, like 911 dispatchers, as first responders. It would also urge Congress to pass the Enhancing First Response Act, which would reclassify them as a protective service job. The resolution says this group plays a key role in emergency response and that the change could affect the benefits and support they can get.

AK-2025-HJR45.s: The Alaska Legislature would urge the U.S. Congress to fully fund the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, which helps pay for special education for students with disabilities. It says federal funding should reach at least 40% of the average per-student cost and stay at that level. The resolution affects students with disabilities, schools, families, and school districts in Alaska.

AK-2025-HJR46.s: A legislative resolution would recognize the choices of the Kipnuk and Kwigillingok communities to move after Typhoon Halong. It would affirm Alaska Native self-determination and urge state and federal help for relocation, including a clear plan, funding, and coordination. It also calls for help with an interim village for the evacuated residents.

AK-2025-SB104.s: The bill would let owners of boats and vehicles add a transfer-on-death title, so the title passes to a named person when the owner dies. It would also let owners of some common interest community ownership interests transfer that property on death. The changes would apply to boat and vehicle owners, and the act would take effect July 1, 2026.

AK-2025-SB130.s: This law changes Alaska’s fisheries product development tax credit, which is a tax break for certain fish business investments. It expands which fish and shellfish can qualify, adds more kinds of equipment and work that can count, and sets rules for how much of the tax bill can be covered and what information is public. It also moves the tax credit’s end date to January 1, 2037, and makes the law retroactive to January 1, 2026.

AK-2025-SB143.s: The bill would require the state education department to give ethics and budget training to school board members who must take it. It would also change the terms of office for municipal school board members and the size of city councils in second class cities. The bill includes an effective date.

AK-2025-SB163.s: It repeals three state funds and accounts, including the public access fund, the Alaska temporary assistance program emergency account, and the 2001 Special Olympics World Winter Games reserve fund. It affects those inactive state accounts and funds. The law took effect on July 4, 2026.

AK-2025-SB164.s: The law ends certain deductions and discounts tied to collecting and remitting the motor fuel tax, tobacco taxes, and tire fees. It would remove the small amount dealers and licensees could keep for filing these returns, and it changes how cigarette stamp refunds and credits are figured. It took effect on July 1, 2026.

AK-2025-SB174.s: Would create the Alaska Invasive Species Council in the Department of Fish and Game to help state, tribal, local, and other groups work together on invasive species. The council would advise on how to manage these species, issue yearly reports and a five-year plan, and oversee a response fund for invasive species work. Members would serve without pay, and the bill would take effect right away if it became law.

AK-2025-SB181.s: This act lets the Labor and Workforce Development Department share certain information with other state agencies, including the University of Alaska, if federal rules allow it. The information can be used for workforce and education data work, program reviews, education outreach, or public policy research. The receiving agency must sign a written agreement and limit any later sharing of the information. It became law without the governor's signature and takes effect October 4, 2026.

AK-2025-SB200.s: The law changes when some service areas can be abolished, replaced, altered, or combined, and it adds voter approval rules with several exceptions for road and fire service areas. It also changes the rules for getting a lower tax assessment on farm land, including the forms, income proof, and what counts as farm use. The service area changes take effect July 1, 2026, and the farm land changes take effect February 1, 2027.

AK-2025-SB208.s: The measure updates state rules for industrial hemp, including registration, testing, fees, transport, and how hemp that tests above the limit can be handled. It also changes rules for the sale and lease of state land for agricultural uses. The bill names the O-S Cross cabbage, also called giant green cabbage, as Alaska’s official state vegetable.

AK-2025-SB214.s: This measure makes state money available for many projects and grants across Alaska. It covers schools, water and sewer systems, housing, transportation, public safety, and airport and aviation work. It also includes capital fund changes and was signed into law.

AK-2025-SB23.s: The bill would require the state education board to post and update free civics teaching materials online for schools to use. It would also bar a high school from giving a diploma unless the student took civics instruction and passed a civics course, test, or project, with some exceptions for transfer students and students with disabilities. The new graduation rule would apply to students who enter grade 9 on or after July 1, 2027.

AK-2025-SB230.s: The law changes the boundaries of some state refuges and fish and game critical habitat areas in Alaska. It also changes the boundary of the Jonesville Public Use Area. The changes affect the listed land and water areas, and the law has its own effective date in the chapter.

AK-2025-SB237.s: The law lets the state issue electronic ID cards, driver’s licenses, and permits on a mobile device to people who already have the physical card or license. It also sets rules for how police and other public safety staff can check them, including limits on searching the phone and protections for damage claims unless there is intentional misconduct. The law also lets the Department of Administration share certain driver and ID data with other government systems and some approved groups for verification, and it took effect on July 7, 2026.

AK-2025-SB239.s: Signed into law in Alaska, this act changes rules for some commercial driver license tests, imported vehicles, and proof of financial responsibility after a judgment. It lets a driver who fails part of a driving test retake only the part they missed. For vehicles at least 25 years old that were legally imported, the state could register and title them without making them meet current federal safety standards, and insurance customers with certain judgment-related suspensions would have new time periods for keeping proof on file.

AK-2025-SB24.s: The bill would raise the age to 21 to buy, trade, or have tobacco, nicotine products, and electronic smoking products. It would also change rules for sales, vending machines, retail cigar stores, and taxes on electronic smoking and vapor products. It would set aside part of state tobacco settlement money for tobacco education and quitting programs.

AK-2025-SB252.s: This law updates Alaska’s rules for commercial deals under the Uniform Commercial Code, including secured transactions, sales, leases, loans, payment records, and money transfers. It also changes how some bonds, titles, and other business papers are treated under state law. The law takes effect on September 30, 2026.

AK-2025-SB282.s: This act changes how Alaska’s Joint Armed Services Committee is set up and what it does. It changes the number and mix of members, adds a yearly meeting with senior military officials, and updates what reports and lists the Legislative Affairs Agency must keep. It also changes some duties tied to military and defense issues and sets new rules for when parts of the law take effect.

AK-2025-SB3001.s: The bill would change taxes and reporting tied to a major natural gas project in Alaska. It would also affect how local school funding is counted, how municipal property taxes work, and how the Alaska Gasline Development Corporation handles some funds. It would create an Alaska affordable heating fuel fund and a municipal impact grant program, and it would set rules for certain contracts, gas price limits, and an alternative tax on natural gas throughput.

AK-2025-SB3002.s: The bill would end Alaska income tax rules for pass-through businesses by repealing the current tax law for them on January 1, 2028. It would affect pass-through entities, such as some partnerships and S corporations, that report income through their owners.

AK-2025-SB63.s: The bill would change the Local Boundary Commission, which handles local area boundary questions, from five members to six. It would change the term for new appointees to six years, while keeping current members' terms the same. The measure would take effect on January 31, 2027, and it was vetoed by the governor.

AK-2025-SB79.s: The law lets employers in Alaska pay wages on a payroll card account if the worker agrees or has not chosen direct deposit. It requires clear notice about card terms and fees, and it gives workers free ways to get their pay and check their balance. The law also bars several fees on the card and says the wages on it must be insured. It took effect on July 1, 2026.

AK-2025-SB86.s: This law updates Alaska rules for businesses that move money for others, including those that handle virtual currency and some payroll processing services. It sets new license rules, renewal steps, record and report duties, and checks for people who control these businesses. It also lets the state work with other states on licensing and enforcement, and it sets rules for abandoned virtual currency and currency exchange licenses.

AK-2025-SCR10.s: This resolution would let lawmakers set aside some state legislative rules so they can consider House Bill 36. That bill is about placing foster children in psychiatric hospitals, caring for children in state custody who are placed in care facilities outside Alaska, and changing a court procedure rule for children in need of aid. It was passed by the legislature.

AK-2025-SCR201.s: This resolution would let the Alaska Senate and House each recess for more than three days during the Second Special Session of the 34th Alaska State Legislature. A concurrent resolution is a formal statement that both chambers must agree to. The resolution was transmitted to the governor and later permanently filed as Legislative Resolve 70.

AK-2025-SCR202.s: The resolution lets certain bills and resolutions carry over from the second regular session to the second special session by setting aside two legislative rules. It applies only to House Bill 381 and Senate Bill 280, which deal with tax rules for certain natural gas pipeline property. It is retroactive to May 21, 2026, at 10:00 a.m.

AK-2025-SCR203.s: The resolution would suspend certain Alaska legislative rules for House Bill 381 so its title can be changed as it moves forward. The bill deals with taxes and fees tied to a natural gas project, school funding, city property taxes, the Alaska Gasline Development Corporation, pipeline reporting, contract approval, gas price limits, and municipal impact grants. The Senate passed the resolution and sent it to the House.

AK-2025-SJR30.s: A legislative resolution is a formal statement, and this one expresses gratitude for the U.S. military and says Alaska supports stronger defense readiness. It supports expanding military bases, shared civilian-and-military projects, and public-private housing deals to help provide housing, roads, utilities, and other needs for service members and families. It also says these efforts could help both defense needs and local communities near bases.
